panels.title: A rock that behaves like a comet
body: Most meteor showers are dust shed by comets, icy balls that crumble as they pass the Sun. The Geminids come from Phaethon instead, a lump of rock only a few kilometres wide.
Today it makes its closest pass of the Sun, far closer than Mercury ever gets. The heat may crack its surface and shed grit, but exactly how it made so much dust is still a puzzle.
details: This moment is Phaethon's closest pass of the Sun (perihelion) in the JPL orbit solution: JD 2461285.6164 TDB, 2 September 2026 at 02:47:40 TDB, about 02:46:31 UTC, rounded down to the minute. The scene moves Phaethon by unperturbed two-body motion from published elements, so near the Sun its place can be off by up to about 935,000 km (see the asteroid's position accuracy); the time is modelled, not observed.
At perihelion Phaethon is about 0.140 AU from the Sun, roughly 21 million km. Mercury's closest distance to the Sun is 46.0 million km.

Size: JPL gives an effective diameter of 6.25 km (Taylor et al. 2019, from radar); NASA's Geminids page gives 5.1 km. Phaethon was discovered on 11 October 1983 by the Infrared Astronomical Satellite.

How Phaethon makes dust is unsettled. NASA's STEREO spacecraft saw it brighten near the Sun in 2009, and Jewitt and Li (2010) proposed that the heat cracks and breaks down its rock. Zhang et al. (2023) found that the brightenings seen near perihelion since 1997 are glowing sodium, not dust, so how the dust of the Geminid stream was shed remains an open question.
sources: NASA/JPL Small-Body Database, 3200 Phaethon (1983 TB): time of perihelion tp = JD 2461285.616438 TDB, perihelion distance q = 0.140278 au, effective diameter 6.25 km (Taylor et al. 2019, Planetary and Space Science, doi 10.1016/j.pss.2019.01.009); https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/sbdb.api?sstr=3200&full-prec=1&phys-par=1 (accessed 2026-10-18)

panels.title: The best shower of the year
body: In early December, Earth starts running into Phaethon's dust. The Geminids are one of the richest and most reliable meteor showers of the year.
On a clear, dark night at their best you might see about two meteors a minute. They get going in mid-evening, too, so you don't have to stay up until dawn.
details: Active 4 to 17 December 2026, peak night 13 to 14 December, zenithal hourly rate 150 (American Meteor Society). NASA gives up to 120 an hour under perfect conditions and 40 to 50 an hour under typical dark skies; "about two a minute" is NASA's 120 an hour.
NASA: the shower "starts around 9 or 10 p.m."

This moment, 6 December 2026 at 00:00 UTC, is two days into the activity, chosen so that the panel opens once the shower has begun, also in the shower-only (activity) view. The rate drawn in the scene is modelled from the published peak rate.
sources: American Meteor Society, Meteor Shower Calendar 2026: Geminids active Dec 4-17, peak night Dec 13-14, ZHR 150; https://www.amsmeteors.org/calendar/ (accessed 2026-10-16)

NASA Science, Geminids: "one of the best and most reliable annual meteor showers"; 120 per hour under perfect conditions, 40 to 50 per hour typical; starts around 9 or 10 p.m.; https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/meteors-meteorites/geminids/ (accessed 2026-10-18)

panels.title: Earth reaches the thickest dust
body: Tonight Earth passes through the busiest part of the stream. Tiny specks of rock hit our air at about 35 km a second and burn up as bright streaks.
They all seem to fly out of Gemini, the Twins, which gives the shower its name.
details: The peak in this scene is 13 December 2026 at 23:31:44 UTC: the moment the Sun reaches solar longitude 261.6° (J2000), the IAU Meteor Data Center's peak, found on the engine's ephemeris. The American Meteor Society's peak night is 13 to 14 December 2026.
Radiant: right ascension 113.0°, declination +32.4° (J2000), in Gemini (IAU Meteor Data Center).
Speed: 35 km a second (22 miles a second), and the meteors tend to look yellow (NASA).
sources: IAU Meteor Data Center, established meteor showers, Geminids (GEM, 4), parameter set AdNo 8 (Jenniskens 2023): peak solar longitude 261.6°, radiant RA 113.0°, Dec +32.4°, J2000; https://www.ta3.sk/IAUC22DB/MDC2022/Etc/streamestablisheddata2026.txt (accessed 2026-10-16)
